subject: strandbeest
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: wind-walking beach creature of tubes.
Style: Theo Jansen kinetic sculpture.

requests.what: Patchwork cloth on both main sails (this part sailL and its twin sailR): SAIL base with a few SAIL_SHADE patches, visible dark seams, sun-bleached edges and a row of sewn reinforcement stitches along the lower edge.
Same weathered cloth for the two small front sails (jibL and jibR): SAIL with faint salt stains and a tan ROPE-coloured hem band along the bottom edge.

Translucent-looking plastic on every back bottle (parts named bottleL0..bottleL6 and bottleR0..bottleR6): BOTTLE with paler fogging, a BOTTLE_DARK ring seam in the middle, and a faint sand dusting near the bottom.
Sun-faded, scuffed yellow conduit on the side rails (railL and railR): YELLOW with YELLOW_DARK scratches, sand scuffs and the odd black marker tick every half metre.
Bottle upper jaw: BOTTLE plastic with a faded printed label band in CAP_BLUE and WHITE, ragged and peeled at one edge.
Cable-tie and bolt clusters where the leg pivots meet the side rail: a washer, nut and two zip ties in DARK and STEEL. Repeat on the first leg unit each side.
A screw-cap with ridged collar on the front end of each back bottle, alternating CAP_BLUE and CAP_ORANGE, plus tiny tie wire loops to the A-frames.
A tattered wind-streamer and weather-vane arrow on top of the main mast: a thin tube arm, a CAP_ORANGE pennant and a small ball finial.
Thin YELLOW batten rods and rope lashings across both main sails, with grommet rings along the leading edge.
Rope rigging: tensioned ROPE lines from mast top to the front and rear of the spine, with small wooden-bead tensioners and a pulley block.
Inside the mouth: a flat DARK fabric tongue strip on the lower jaw and two small cork 'fangs' at the lower jaw front.
Expressive brows over both eyes: bent thin yellow tubes with a zip-tie knot on the outer end, giving a curious look.
Flat sandal-like pads under the leg feet: DARK rubber discs with three small STEEL bolts, one per foot, on the rear four legs.

calls.reasoning:
I'm planning out a Strandbeest-style wind creature with yellow conduit-like tube legs using Jansen linkages, white sail fabric, and bottle-shaped wind stomachs, aiming to keep the module compact and skeleton-first in its construction.

I'll build each leg by positioning its crank, pivot, and joint points using circle-intersection math to approximate the standard Jansen linkage proportions, mirroring the frame across both sides with phase offsets per leg pair along the body length.

Picking plausible intersection constructions for each linkage node, choosing upper/lower branch signs so the mechanism stays consistent and avoids invalid (NaN) intersections.

Then I'll compute the overall scale factor to map the Jansen linkage units to meters and figure out where the foot lands, shifting the whole leg vertically so the lowest foot across all legs rests at ground level.

For the body frame, I'm planning the side rails, crank axle tubes, crossbeams, and central spine, plus a wing/sail structure and a row of bottles mounted on top like ballast or decoration.

I also want to give the creature a face: a bundle at the front forming a snout with upper and lower jaw tubes, plus round eyes made from bottle caps. For the joint hierarchy, I'll set up a root "body" joint, a "jaw" joint, and a "leg" role joint per leg chain, each parented to the body at the hip, with rods connecting the bones.

Now I'm setting up the rig: a root body joint at the proper height, leg joints at each hip tagged with a "leg" role, and a rod helper function to draw tubes between joints. I'm adding small sphere connectors at each node to mimic the bolts and cable ties on Jansen's mechanisms.

For the leg geometry, I'm placing each unit with paired planes per side (inner and outer x offsets) to avoid z-fighting, spacing five units along the z-axis, and offsetting the phase between left and right sides by 180 degrees so the legs move in a walking pattern.

Now I'm working out the Jansen linkage nodes themselves — hip pivot, crank axle, crank radius, and the connecting rods that define points B, D, E, F using trilateration from the known joint distances, keeping the total rod and sphere count for ten legs within budget.

Checking the D-E-F triangle (36.7, 49, 65.7) confirms it's valid, and the K-E-D triangle works too as long as |KD| falls within range, so I'll proceed with the fallback. Now listing the full rod set: C–K, K–B, A–B, A–D, B–D, K–E, D–E, D–F, E–F, plus the foot tip.

I'm adding a small foot cap at F to represent a shoe, then computing the overall height by finding the lowest point across all leg nodes relative to A at the origin -- taking the max of negative F.y plus foot radius. For mirroring left and right legs, I'm keeping the forward direction consistent along +z. For the body, I'm positioning side rails at the leg plane offset in x, raised slightly above the foot height along z.

Now I'm placing the hip pivot axle as a rod spanning across x at height H, then the crank axle rod offset further out and raised by the crank length, acting as the bent axle that drives the mechanism. For the upper frame, I'm laying out side rails and a central top spine rod running along z at an elevated y, with triangular strut frames connecting the spine down to the rails and legs for structural support.

Then I'm adding decorative bottles on top as small translucent cylinders arranged in two rows along the spine, and sketching sail panels at the back as trapezoidal extruded shapes mounted on a mast to give the piece a windmill/sailboat character.

Now I'm designing the head: a neck rod rising forward from the spine front to a head position, then building the skull from a horizontal white bottle as the snout/upper jaw with a separate lower jaw piece.

For eyes I'm placing spheres with blue cap discs and black pupils on top of the upper jaw's front, and setting up a bone hierarchy where the head joint parents the body and the jaw is a child.

I'm also defining the full color palette (yellow, white, sail, bottle blue, cap blue/orange, dark, rope) as top-level constants, and designing the feet as sphere shoes with dark rubber soles and rings, plus bolts for joints.

Now I'm thinking through texture requests for each part—patchwork and sun-bleached stripes for sails, peeling labels and fogging for bottles, weathering and scuffs for the yellow conduits—and naming parts consistently so textures can target them, though I'm realizing I need concrete numeric height values for the "at" coordinates rather than leaving them computed dynamically.

I'm working out the leg scaling so the foot lands at a fixed target height: scale factor S derived from target hip height minus foot radius, divided by the unscaled leg span. Checking proportions against a real strandbeest's ~3m height, adjusting sail height to around 1.1 so overall silhouette doesn't get too tall, and computing the resulting scale factor to see how small the leg crank offsets become.

Now I'm checking whether adjacent leg units would collide—since Jansen legs alternate planes, I need units spaced far enough apart in x, with odd/even units offset onto different planes so their reach doesn't overlap, and figuring out where the rails and crank axle should sit relative to that spacing.

With H=0.95 fixed, I'm computing key coordinates: spine height, z range for the walking motion, and head position. Now I'm starting to write the TypeScript code to build this, setting up imports from the 3js builder library and defining a function to compute leg node positions.

I'm writing the circle-intersection helper that finds the two possible points where two circles meet, then using it to derive the Jansen linkage joints A through D by chaining distance constraints from the crank position K.

Checking B's position against the distance constraints, the numbers are roughly consistent, so I'll continue with approximate coordinates and move on to locating D using the same intersection method with A and B as reference points.

Picking lower-left for D, then computing E and F by intersecting the leg lengths, choosing the side that keeps them lower each time. The overall height ends up around 70-90 units, which doesn't need to be physically realistic, so I'll just take the minimum vertical position across all nodes to set the ground reference.

Now I'm working out the leg phase angles per unit and side, then mapping those into world positions for each joint by combining the pivot point with the computed offsets. I'm setting up the joint hierarchy for each leg with rod and bolt geometry, crank coloring, and the rail/beam structure connecting pivots to the rail at each side.

I'm working out the axle positions across different leg units to check for clutter, then placing the body's root joint and starting to figure out where the head joint and neck rods should attach relative to the front rails.

Now I'm designing the head geometry: capsules for upper and lower jaws, small cone teeth lining the upper jaw, and sphere eyes with blue cap pupils.

Now I'm positioning the bottles along the A-frame slopes, calculating where they rest on the frame lines at roughly x=±0.28, y=1.3, and laying out two rows of seven bottles spaced about 0.46 apart along z.

Next I'm placing the A-frame supports at five z-positions, building rods from the base posts up to the apex, adding yellow crossbeams and top rails, plus diagonal braces between frames for structural detail.

For the sails, I'm planning a central mast with two sail panels extruded as curved outlines on either side, using a thin thickness and sail shapes that taper upward toward a point to look like triangular canvas.

Still thinking through boom rods along the sail bottom, a second smaller jib-style sail toward the front with its own mast, rope rods connecting the mast top to the front spine, and rubber-textured feet with sphere caps for the tips. I'm also sketching out naming conventions for the texture requests so each sail part matches its material.

Setting up the joint hierarchy now—root body joint, leg joints with downward direction, and head/jaw joints parented appropriately with their attach points and orientations.

I'm defining a rod helper and sphere part helper to simplify building limbs and body parts, then placing the eyes: white sphere sockets, blue iris spheres, and black pupils positioned above the jaw line.

I'm planning careful, minimal edits using the paint utility functions from the SDK, starting with updating the import statement to include the helper functions I'll need like noise, mix, smoothstep, and cells.

Then I'm working out how to define sail paints that use cell patterns for patches, distance-based seams for dark lines, and periodic dashes near the bottom edge for stitching, likely needing separate functions for the main sail and the jib since their scales differ, and swapping the hardcoded color logic for a proper paint selection based on which sail panel it is.

For the bottle capsule, I'm sketching a fog-noise paint with a seam ring at the midpoint of the path and a sand blend near the bottom, alternating between two base colors depending on which side. For the rail, I'm planning distance markers every half meter along the rod's length, plus stretched noise for scratches and a sandy color mix blended in near the surface.

Now I'm working out the snout geometry as a capsule with a label band section featuring a ragged peeled edge using noise offsets, blue coloring with white stripes, and text-like tick marks, with noise cuts revealing the underlying bottle color where the peel effect is strongest. I'm now editing the actual bottle and snout capsule definitions to apply these color and paint choices.

Checking the rail line's color type -- since the rod helper expects a string parameter, passing a Paint object would fail typechecking, so I'm loosening the helper's signature to accept `any` for the color argument.
